Thank you for sending your work entitled “3D Modelling of microtubules, flows and mRNA transport in Drosophila reveals transitions in cytoskeletal organization” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Diethard Tautz (Senior editor) and 3 reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The Reviewing editor and the other reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

This manuscript presents a stochastic theoretical model of microtubule nucleation and growth to study the spatial organization of the 3D cortex of the Drosophila oocyte. The key finding of the work is that a simple gradient of microtubule nucleation along the lateral surface naturally leads to the formation of a microtubule network that looks like the one seen in the oocyte and that can guide oscar and unprocessed bicoid mRNA to the specific points in the cell where they are found. The authors also show that cytoplasmic streaming occurs but plays no role in positioning.

This work is interesting and novel. However the referees were not fully convinced that the work is of sufficient general interest for publication in eLife. The impression that the work might be mainly of interest for specialists could stem from the presentation of the work which is difficult to read. In particular, it is difficult to understand what exactly are the key findings of the paper. Despite these problems the referees have agreed to give the authors the opportunity to revise their manuscript as the work is very interesting and contributes novel ideas. It provides a systematic approach to determine which transport mechanisms are at work or may be at work. So far this has been quite unclear and there was much speculation. However the authors have to demonstrate in a revised manuscript that their work is of general interest before this submission could be suitable for eLife. The authors should revise their manuscript taking into account the points raised below.

Specific criticism:

– in general, this paper is quite hard to digest. A lot of information is provided but the reader is not really well assisted to make sense of this information. It is difficult to extract what it is exactly the authors find out with their work. The logic of the arguments is overall not very clearly laid out, even though the models are well explained. Some of the issues raised below might even be addressed somewhere in the manuscript but I did not find these points clarified.

– The authors show that when averaging over many realizations of the MT network, a clear pattern of direction bias emerges inside the cell (Figure 1F). However it remains unclear whether a single realization that would correspond to a real oocyte is good enough. Would the bias in single realization be good enough to position the mRNA properly? I understand that on average the proposed mechanism would work. But this is not the same as saying it works essentially every time. This is a real worry about the paper that the authors do not address.

– The authors calculate cytoplasmic flow patterns using a force distribution obtained from the MT models. In general, flows might influence the cytoskeleton and change its structure. Are there good reasons to neglect such effects? Could such effects be important?

Where I would like to have seen a little more explanation is around Equation (1), when the authors introduce the force field f. They vaguely write that it results from motor-driven transport. The authors do not specify what is transported and why the net flow only results from motors of one kind (dyneins and kinesins might segregate and generate flows of different strengths in different compartments of the oocyte). I would like to invite the authors to discuss in more detail the assumptions underlying their choice of f.

– The discussion of “normal” and “untreated” bicoid mRNA is unclear. It is interesting that the model can account for the behavior of injected “untreated” bicoid mRNA. Also the failure of the model to explain the behavior of normal mRNA is very interesting but it also raises many interesting questions. Unfortunately the discussion of these facts is quite unclear and only paragraph 16 of the Result section is this important distinction (normal versus untreated) introduced. In the figure caption this distinction is not mentioned. I think it would help preparing this issue in the Introduction and it is important to discuss the implications of this result carefully.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled “Cortical microtubule nucleation can organise the cytoskeleton of Drosophila oocytes to define the anteroposterior axis” for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Diethard Tautz (Senior editor) and a Reviewing editor.

There are still some comments from the Reviewing Editor that should be addressed to optimize the final manuscript:

The authors have significantly improved the manuscript. Important points are now clarified and the revised manuscript is much better to read. Before the manuscript can be finally accepted, the authors should consider the following points and suggestions for clarification.

An important point is the statement the MT network “turns over rapidly”.

This clarifies the issue about the possibility of the system to average

over many realizations of stochastic microtubule networks. The authors do

not give an estimate for the turnover time. Rather they imply that since

MT's in the presence of colchicine disappear “within minutes” this suggests “rapid” turnover. However, this is not very clear. Since colchicine is a MT-depolymerizing drug the most simple interpretation could be that MT's disappear because of direct colchicine-triggered depolymerization. Therefore the argument for rapid turnover should be more carefully explained and it would be useful to state what estimated values/ranges for the MT turnover time the authors use.

The authors state in the Results that they “cycled through the pairs of fluid flow and motor-velocities...” It is not very clear what this means. I interpret this statement as describing an alternation between generating a new MT meshwork and solving Equation (1) for this network and then during a short time interval solving (2) with constant flow velocity u - and repeating this procedure. However this should be explained. What are the time-intervals chosen and is this choice relevant for the results?

In the Results section sixteenth paragraph, the authors discuss results for naive bicoid simulations shown in Figure 3 H and I. It remains unclear here what experimental observations are and whether “splitting” suggested in the model can be seen experimentally. Note also that the sentences in this paragraph are written such that it is sometimes difficult to understand whether they refer to experiments or to calculations. I also found it difficult to find information in the text about the exact differences between naive and endogenous bicoid in experiments.

In the Results section the sentence “However the model does not reproduce transport specifically to the anterior surface when injection is further away from the anterior” is not completely clear. Is it correct to say: “...when injection of conditioned bicoid is further away”? That would be clearer.

results.result: The computational polymer model of the MT cytoskeleton, based on cortical nucleation with a steep posterior-to-anterior gradient, reproduces key experimental observations including MT density distribution, directional bias (8.5% posterior bias in 3D), and depth-dependent variations in 2D slices.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 and C13 collectively demonstrate that the polymer model successfully recapitulates experimental MT distributions and directional biases. The model parameters are constrained by experimental measurements (C2, Figure 1D), and computational outputs (C4, C5) match published experimental data with appropriate quantitative agreement. The depth-dependent variation (C6) provides additional validation.

results.result: 2D confocal measurements inadequately characterize the 3D MT system, and the oocyte samples many independent MT network configurations over stage 9 due to rapid turnover.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is directly supported by the computational demonstration of depth-dependent directional bias (C6). Claim C10 follows logically from the Colchicine experiment data (C8, C9) showing 5-10 min turnover time combined with the 6-9 hr duration of stage 9, yielding tens to hundreds of independent configurations.

results.result: The MT network turns over within minutes, as demonstrated by Colchicine treatment causing MT disappearance in 5-10 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C9 are supported by multiple literature citations and personal communication. The inference that complete network turnover occurs within minutes (C9) is reasonable given that Colchicine blocks MT growth and the entire visible network disappears in 5-10 min.

results.result: Ensemble averaging over 50 independent realizations reveals that the MT cytoskeleton is organized in a compartmental fashion with distinct spatial domains: posterior-pointing at the anterior and inward-pointing at lateral sides. This organization is robust to model parameters and geometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C17 describe the emergence of compartmental organization from ensemble averaging. The computational results (C11, C12, Figure 1F) are internally consistent, and robustness testing (C14, C15) strengthens the conclusion. The finding that disordered arrays can have well-defined mean organizations (C16, C17) represents a key conceptual advance supported by both polymer and rod models.

results.result: Computed cytoplasmic flow fields derived from the MT cytoskeleton model are consistent with experimentally observed slow flows, being strongest in the anterior half and weaker posteriorly, with flows driven by kinesin-dependent transport serving as a secondary readout of cytoskeletal organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C26 establish consistency between computed and experimental flows. The model is calibrated to match experimental flow speeds (C21, Figure 2F), and qualitative patterns agree (C22). Minor discrepancies are acknowledged (C23), and the negligible impact of the nucleus (C25) is quantified. The conclusion that flows are secondary readouts (C20, C26) is supported by the kinesin-dependence (C18, C19).

results.result: Simulations of oskar mRNA transport reproduce experimental localization patterns including transient channel formation and posterior crescent accumulation without requiring anchoring, with 12.5% of cargo localizing to a 4 μm posterior slice, demonstrating that continual transport with slow diffusion is sufficient for localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C36 describe oskar mRNA transport simulations. The model parameters are constrained by experimental data (C27, C28), and simulation results match experimental observations at multiple time points (C29, C31, C34). The quantitative localization efficiency (C35: 12.5%) is substantial. The exclusion of anchoring (C32, C33) is justified by experimental evidence, and the conclusion about sufficiency (C36) follows from the simulation results.

results.result: Motor-driven cytoskeletal transport is both necessary and sufficient for oskar mRNA localization, while cytoplasmic flows play a negligible role, as demonstrated by simulations showing 11.3% localization without flows versus complete failure without motors, and only 2.7% localization with flows alone even with a perfect anchor.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C42 systematically test the contributions of different transport mechanisms. The simulations show that removing flows has minimal impact (C37, C38: 11.3% vs 12.5%), removing motors causes complete failure (C40), and flows with a perfect anchor achieve only 2.7% localization (C41). These results strongly support the necessity and sufficiency conclusion (C42), though the idealized anchor test (C41) may overestimate flow contribution.

results.result: Simulations of naive bicoid mRNA transport (using Dynein-mediated minus-end directed transport) successfully reproduce experimental injection results, with mRNA accumulating at cortical regions nearest the injection site or splitting between regions when placed at compartment boundaries, supporting the compartmental organization of the MT cytoskeleton.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 describe bicoid mRNA simulations. The model appropriately inverts motor direction for Dynein (C43), and simulation results match experimental injection patterns (C44-C46). The independence from flows (C47) and the mechanistic explanation via compartment boundaries (C48) are consistent with the MT organization. The agreement between simulations and experiments (C49, C50) provides strong validation of the compartmental model.

results.result: The model reproduces endogenous bicoid mRNA localization to anterior corners but fails to capture the specific anterior targeting of conditioned bicoid mRNA from distant injection sites, suggesting involvement of unidentified MT populations or MT-independent mechanisms dependent on Exuperantia.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 show partial success in modeling endogenous bicoid, while C55-C56 acknowledge a significant limitation. The model captures local anterior localization (C53, C54) but not long-range specific targeting (C55). The speculation about Exuperantia mechanisms (C56) is reasonable but unresolved. This represents an important limitation that requires future work to address.

results.result: Cortical MT nucleation gradients are sufficient to assemble a functional compartmentalized cytoskeleton, and the model successfully reproduces the clone-adjacent mislocalisation phenotype by adding MT nucleation sites to one side of the posterior pole.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 summarizes the main finding, supported by all previous results. Claims C58-C60 test the model against a specific mutant phenotype. The simulation (C60) reproduces the experimental observation (C59) by modulating MT nucleation, providing additional validation of the model's explanatory power.

results.result: Simulations with uniform posterior MT nucleation (mimicking strong par-1 hypomorphs) reproduce the central mislocalisation of oskar mRNA observed in ~90% of mutant oocytes, with MTs pointing toward a single central stable focus and directional bias eliminated.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C67 describe par-1 mutant simulations. The model appropriately implements uniform posterior nucleation (C64) based on experimental observations (C61-C63), and simulation results (C65, C66) match the experimental phenotype (C63). The robustness to slight variations in posterior nucleation (C67) is consistent with the range of hypomorph severities.

results.result: Simulations predict and experiments confirm that bicoid mRNA mislocalizes to both anterior corners and posterior pole in strong par-1 hypomorphs, matching EGFR mutant phenotypes, demonstrating that near-uniform MT nucleation explains polarity defects in multiple mutant backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 provide a strong prediction-validation cycle. The model predicts bicoid mislocalisation (C68), which matches EGFR mutants (C69), and new experimental data confirm the prediction for par-1 hypomorphs (C70). The conclusion that uniform MT nucleation explains multiple mutant phenotypes (C71) is well-supported by the convergent evidence.

results.result: Intermediate levels of posterior MT nucleation create a cytoskeleton with both stable and unstable fixed points separated by a potential barrier, explaining partial mislocalisation phenotypes where oskar mRNA splits between posterior pole and central dot, with diffusion and flows potentially aiding transport across the barrier.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 describe intermediate phenotypes. The experimental observation (C72) is reproduced by simulations with intermediate nucleation parameters (C73, C74), and the mechanistic interpretation via stable/unstable fixed points (C75) is consistent with dynamical systems theory. The role of diffusion and flows in crossing barriers (C77) is a reasonable inference, and the summary conclusion (C78) is well-supported.

results.result: The transition from wild-type to par-1 hypomorph cytoskeletal topology constitutes a saddle-node bifurcation with cortical MT seeding density as the bifurcation parameter, and MT length emerges as a second bifurcation parameter, establishing both as key regulators of non-centrosomal network polarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 provide mathematical characterization of the system. The saddle-node bifurcation identification (C79) is supported by the mathematical analysis (Figure 4K-M), and the discovery of MT length as a second bifurcation parameter (C80) is demonstrated computationally. The mechanistic explanations (C81, C82) are logical, and the conclusion about key regulators (C83) follows from the parameter space analysis.

results.result: The three-dimensional model demonstrates that a simple gradient of cortical MT nucleation is sufficient to reproduce MT distribution, flow patterns, and mRNA localizations, excludes a major role for cytoplasmic flows, reveals more ordered cytoskeletal organization than previously thought, and explains mutant phenotypes through bifurcations in cytoskeletal organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 represent the main conclusions of the study, summarizing findings from all previous results. Each conclusion is supported by multiple lines of evidence: sufficiency of MT gradients (C84) by successful reproduction of multiple phenotypes, exclusion of flow role (C85) by systematic testing, ordered organization (C86) by ensemble averaging, bifurcation explanation (C87) by mutant simulations, and overall significance (C88) by the comprehensive explanatory power of the model.
